messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 24
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: South Asian
- Relationship Status: In a relationship
- Occupation: Diplomat
- Trauma Type: Civilian in war zone
- Pcl5: 66

He is a 24-year-old South Asian man who has spent most of his adult life trying to be composed in rooms where other people look to him for steadiness. As a diplomat, he is trained to be careful with language, to notice shifts in tone, to keep his face neutral. That skill, once a source of pride, now feels like part of the problem. He says he learned to perform calm so well that even when he is frightened, the fear arrives silently, without warning and without permission.

His difficulties begin after he is sent to work in a conflict-affected region as a civilian representative. At first, he feels energized by the responsibility. He is young, ambitious, and proud to be trusted. He remembers telling his partner before departure that this assignment would matter, that it would prove something. In the war zone, however, the world becomes disordered in ways he cannot anticipate. There are days when the roads are closed, power disappears, and the sound of explosions is so ordinary that people stop speaking when they hear them. He describes learning to scan windows, doorways, rooftops, and crowds without thinking about it. His body stays tense from morning to night, as if bracing for impact. He begins sleeping lightly, shoes near the bed, passport and phone always within reach.

The event that changes him is not one dramatic moment but a sequence that collapses into a single memory. He is in transit between offices when gunfire erupts nearby and the vehicle stops abruptly. People begin shouting. He remembers the smell of dust and fuel, the heat inside the car, and the shock of realizing that his training offers no useful script for what is happening. He crouches low, unable to tell whether the shots are close or far, and waits in a state of disbelief that quickly turns into terror. Later, when he is moved to safety, he notices that his hands are shaking so badly he cannot hold his phone. He keeps checking his body for injuries he cannot find. For days after, he cannot stop replaying the scene, especially the moment of not knowing whether he would live.

After that, he starts to experience the world as unstable and dangerous in a way that follows him home. He returns from assignments carrying the same tension in his shoulders and jaw, but now the alertness no longer switches off. He jumps at sirens, slamming doors, helicopters, and sudden laughter in public places. At night, he wakes with his heart racing, often before he can remember what he dreamed. He avoids war footage, news alerts, and even conversations with colleagues about violence abroad because they pull him immediately back into the vehicle, the gunfire, the feeling that the next second might be his last. He also avoids sitting with his back to open spaces and instinctively chooses seats where he can see exits, a habit he says feels embarrassing but impossible to resist.

He is troubled by intrusive images that arrive when he is trying to work or spend time with his partner. Sometimes it is the sound first, not the picture—an imagined crack, a burst of noise—followed by a flash of the car, the road, the dust. He grows irritable and withdrawn, then feels guilty for snapping at people he loves. He notices that he has become less interested in social plans, less able to relax, less able to feel present. Even on safe days, part of him remains in the war zone, waiting for the next threat. He says he feels ashamed that he cannot simply “move on,” especially because he is expected to be resilient and articulate. Instead, he finds himself exhausted by the effort of appearing normal.

In sessions, he speaks with restraint but with visible strain, as though each detail costs him something. He wants to protect his family and partner from worrying, so he minimizes how bad it is. Yet he also admits that the distance he feels from other people has become harder to hide. He loves his partner and values the stability of the relationship, but he feels internally split between the life he is supposed to be building and the part of him that still lives in constant anticipation of danger. He remains able to function at work, but it is a narrow functioning, maintained by vigilance, caffeine, long hours, and the habit of pushing feelings aside until they return in the dark.
